records.label: Patient with cryohydrocytosis

phenotypes.text: increased erythrocyte membrane permeability to Na and K
absent band 7 protein 22 x 8 in erythrocyte membranes

quotes: We investigated the erythrocyte membrane proteins of two patients with congenital hemolytic anemia due to increased permeability of the erythrocyte membrane to Na and K (hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis).
In the patients with hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis, 22 x 8 was completely absent, whereas 60 x 8 was detected as usual.

records.label: Two stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis cases

phenotypes.text: stomatin deficiency in red cell membranes
abnormal intracellular Na+ and K+ concentrations

quotes: two showed a minimum at around 20-25 degrees C, such that the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C, giving the phenotype known as 'cryohydrocytosis'. These patients are the only two known cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis.
Both showed a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts and massive hepatosplenomegaly, probably defining a new haemato-neurological syndrome.

records.label: 2 previously reported sdCHC cases
quotes: We have previously reported 2 cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis (sdCHC), a rare form of stomatocytosis associated with a cold-induced cation leak, hemolytic anemia, and hepatosplenomegaly but also with cataracts, seizures, mental retardation, and movement disorder.
On the basis of a 3-dimensional model of glut1, we propose potential mechanisms underlying the phenotypes of the 2 mutations found.

records.label: Proband (infant)

phenotypes.text: extremely leaky red cells with temperature-dependent potassium loss

variants.as_reported: trinucleotide deletion in SLC2A1, coding for the deletion of isoleucine 435 or 436 in GLUT1

quotes: The infant presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction, and microcephaly. Later, seizures occurred and developmental milestones were delayed.

Magnetic resonance imaging and computerized tomography scans of the brain showed multiple abnormalities including periventricular calcification. Visual impairment was present due to the presence of both cataracts and retinal dysfunction.
A trinucleotide deletion in SLC2A1, coding for the deletion of isoleucine 435 or 436 in GLUT1, was identified in the proband.

notes.statement: Bawazir et al. (2012) found that the red cells of the proband were extremely leaky to cations, causing hemolysis, and showed temperature-dependent loss of potassium, explaining the hyperkalemia as pseudohyperkalemia.
quotes: Measurements of red cell cation content showed extremely leaky red cells (causing the hemolysis) and temperature-dependent loss of potassium from red cells (explaining the hyperkalemia as pseudohyperkalemia).

notes.statement: Bawazir et al. (2012) suggested that the multisystem pathology probably reflects a combination of glucose transport deficiency at the blood-brain barrier, as in typical GLUT1 deficiency, and the deleterious osmotic effects of a cation-leaky membrane protein in cells expressing GLUT1, notably the red cell. They noted this was the fourth pedigree described with the syndrome.
quotes: This is the fourth pedigree to be described with this most unusual syndrome. The multisystem pathology probably reflects a combination of glucose transport deficiency at the blood-brain barrier (as in typical GLUT1 deficiency) and the deleterious osmotic effects of a cation-leaky membrane protein in the cells where GLUT1 is expressed, notably the red cell.

notes.statement: Flatt et al. (2011) found that stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis was associated with mutations in SLC2A1, and expression studies in Xenopus oocytes showed that the mutations caused both loss of glucose transport and a cation leak. They proposed possible mechanisms for the 2 mutations' phenotypes based on a 3-dimensional model of GLUT1.
quotes: We now show that sdCHC is associated with mutations in SLC2A1 that cause both loss of glucose transport and a cation leak, as shown by expression studies in Xenopus oocytes.
On the basis of a 3-dimensional model of glut1, we propose potential mechanisms underlying the phenotypes of the 2 mutations found.

notes.statement: Flatt et al. (2011) found that stomatin was lost from erythroid cells during reticulocyte maturation, through a process involving endocytosis.
quotes: We investigated the loss of stomatin during erythropoiesis and find this occurs during reticulocyte maturation and involves endocytosis.

notes.statement: Fricke et al. (2004) described 5 cases of stomatin-deficient hereditary stomatocytosis that differed in the temperature dependence of the passive K+ leak. Three showed a simple monotonic temperature dependence. In the other 2, the leak was lowest at about 20 to 25 degrees C and the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C (cryohydrocytosis). Both of these patients had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts, and massive hepatosplenomegaly, which the authors suggested probably defined a new haemato-neurologic syndrome.
quotes: The cases differed markedly between themselves with regard to the temperature dependence of the passive leak to K(+). Three showed a simple monotonic temperature dependence, while two showed a minimum at around 20-25 degrees C
Both showed a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts and massive hepatosplenomegaly, probably defining a new haemato-neurological syndrome.

notes.statement: Fricke et al. (2004) found by Western blotting that red cell membranes were deficient in stomatin in all cases. Immunocytochemistry showed that the deficiency was incomplete: on blood films, some red cells were stomatin-positive and most were negative, although in 1 case only a minority were negative. All platelets and neutrophils were stomatin-positive.
quotes: In all cases, Western blotting of red cell membranes revealed a deficiency in the 32 kDa membrane protein, stomatin.

On typical blood films, some red cells showed positive stomatin immunoreactivity, while most were negative, although in one case only a minority were negative. All platelets and neutrophils were stomatin positive.

notes.statement: Lande et al. (1982) used SDS gel electrophoresis to separate the erythrocyte membrane band 7 into 3 components (about 30, 28, and 26 kD). The 28-kD component was decreased in a patient with hereditary stomatocytosis and in a patient with cryohydrocytosis. On 2-dimensional electrophoresis, the 28-kD component separated into 2 proteins, 22 x 8 and 60 x 8. Protein 22 x 8 was completely absent in both patients, while 60 x 8 was present as usual.
quotes: The 28,000-dalton component was decreased in both patients with permeability disorders.
In the patients with hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis, 22 x 8 was completely absent, whereas 60 x 8 was detected as usual.

notes.statement: Lande et al. (1982) found that all band 7 proteins, including 22 x 8, were present in every normal subject and reticulocytosis control they surveyed. They suggested that absence of this protein might be responsible for the increased Na and K permeability in hereditary stomatocytosis and cryohydrocytosis.
quotes: In contrast, all the band 7 proteins (including 22 x 8) were invariably present in a survey of normal subjects and reticulocytosis controls.
raises the possibility that the absence of this protein is responsible for the increased Na and K permeability in these disorders
